subject: AI stocks fell 10% and the Fed still wants to hike
bodyMarkdown:
If you hold any US index fund inside an RRSP or a TFSA, last week took a real bite out of it, and the rescue people keep expecting is not on the way. The Fed and the Bank of Canada both decide on December 9, and both are talking about raising rates rather than cutting them.

## What happened on Friday

The S&P 500 closed Friday at 6,910.39, down 3.7% on the day and 8.6% for the week, its worst week since April 2025. That was a seventh straight losing session, and it left the index in a **correction**, meaning more than 10% below its record close on October 6. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.3% on the day to 22,617.73 and lost 10% over the week, its worst since March 2020, which wiped out its gain for the year. Nvidia did most of the damage. It dropped 14% to $125.53 after Reuters reported on Friday that SEC enforcement staff are examining the company's accounting, erasing close to $500 billion of market value in one session. Anthropic, which priced its IPO at $83 a share and closed its first day of trading on Thursday at $97.17, gave back more than 8% on Friday.

## Nobody is coming to cut rates

Every AI wobble this year has run into the same assumption, that if stocks fall far enough, central banks will ease to catch them. Read what the committees are actually saying. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, and the Associated Press reported on Wednesday that the minutes of that meeting showed nearly all officials expecting a quarter point increase in December. Kalshi's market on the December meeting still priced a hike near 90% late last week. The Bank of Canada raised its own policy rate to 2.50% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and the summary of deliberations published on November 10 said the governing council may need to go further, carefully. Inflation is the reason. Statistics Canada reported on November 16 that CPI held at 3.1% in October for a second month.

## The Canadian side of it

Our central bank is in a stranger spot than the Fed. The Bank of Canada sits at 2.50%, more than a full point below the Fed's range, and this month it renewed its agreement with Ottawa to target 2% inflation measured by the headline consumer price index, the number currently printing 3.1%. That renewal is a signal about which way the governing council leans when markets get loud. Its next decision is December 9, five days before the November CPI figure arrives on December 14, so the council will move or hold without having seen it. Overnight trading in Asia showed how thin the recovery is. Korea's KOSPI fell nearly 6% at its low before paring the loss to around 3%, Taiwan gained roughly 2% on government support, China loosened its margin financing rules, Japan was closed for a holiday, and US futures were up about 2% as I wrote this. A 2% bounce does not undo a 10% week.

## The takeaway

Put December 9 in your calendar, because the Fed and the Bank of Canada both report that morning, and a hike from either one reaches variable mortgages and lines of credit within weeks. Watch whether the Nvidia story turns into anything official, since an accounting question at the company carrying the whole index is a different animal from an argument about valuation. If you have been buying US technology through an index fund without looking, go check what share of your money sits in one sector now, while the number is still fresh. And if you are young and still adding, a cheaper market is the half of this you should be happy about.
